questions.text: Is the record versioned? Does the keeper keep superseded states, or only the current snapshot?
Are the categories dated? Does each category carry the date it came into existence, and does each assignment carry the date it was made?
Is the writing coupled to the outcome? Is the record completed, reviewed or enriched on the schedule of the outcome it is later used to explain?
Is a second vintage a join? Can two versions of the same records be read side by side without a new data collection?

asks.text: Ask when the measure was written, not only what it says: whether the categories and assignments existed at the event they are dated to.
If the artefact is versioned, read two versions and state which one an estimate comes from; a second version is a join, not a new data collection.
If it is not versioned, ask whether the writing is coupled to the outcome, because coupling, not revision, does the damage.

report.text: A count of first-time pairs also counts how broadly a document has been classified, itself a product of maintenance, so breadth belongs in the reported model.

A level read from the current record moves by more than its own size across defensible states of the record, whereas a difference can remove a component common to both its sides, a protection argued here, not demonstrated.
State which state of the record each estimate is read from.

keeper.text: Date assignments, so that the timing of a category on a record is recorded rather than proved from the category’s own validity date.
Keep superseded states as first-class objects rather than by-products of a snapshot.
Accuracy is a separate question from vintage; the two defects need different remedies, and only the undated one is this paper’s subject.

not_to_conclude: The current version is not wrong. It is a record maintained for the work of the present, and it does that job. The error is reading it as a history without saying at which date it is read.
